title: Gradle, the Wrapper, and Android Build Flow

scout.purpose: The build system converts source and resources into verified artifacts; understanding its configuration and task graph makes failures actionable.
scout.realWorldUse: Every Android compile, test, lint, package, bundle, install, and CI action is represented by Gradle tasks configured by the Android Gradle Plugin.
scout.outcome: Explain wrapper, Gradle, plugin, task, dependency, and cache roles, then trace an Android build from configuration through packaging.

sections.title: The wrapper selects Gradle; plugins teach it Android

blocks.text: Gradle is a general build automation engine. The Gradle wrapper consists of checked-in scripts and configuration that download and run the project’s declared Gradle distribution, giving developers and CI the same version without a global install. The Android Gradle Plugin, or AGP, adds Android concepts such as build types, source sets, manifest processing, resources, APKs, and app bundles. Kotlin plugins add Kotlin compilation. These versions have compatibility relationships with the JDK and Android Studio, so upgrade them intentionally from official compatibility guidance. Running ./gradlew from the repository uses the wrapper; invoking a random system gradle may silently select a different engine.

blocks.caption: The wrapper reports its environment, exposes configured tasks, and executes one exact module task with useful failure context.

sections.title: Configuration creates a task graph; execution builds requested outputs

blocks.text: Gradle first initialises the build and evaluates settings, then configures projects and tasks, then executes the requested task graph. A task declares inputs, outputs, and dependencies on other tasks. Asking for assembleDebug causes prerequisite compilation, resource processing, manifest merging, dexing, and packaging tasks to run as needed. Incremental builds and the build cache avoid repeating work when declared inputs and outputs prove it safe. A clean build deletes outputs and is useful for specific stale-artifact questions, but routinely cleaning defeats incremental feedback and does not repair incorrect configuration. Read the first failed task and its root diagnostic before the long cascade of skipped work.

sections.title: Dependencies are resolved from declared repositories

blocks.text: A dependency declaration identifies coordinates and a configuration such as implementation, testImplementation, or debugImplementation. Gradle resolves metadata and artifacts from configured repositories, applies version selection, and constructs compile/runtime classpaths. Dependency failures may be network access, unavailable coordinates, repository policy, incompatible bytecode, or duplicate classes—not one generic “Gradle problem.” Version catalogs can centralise names and versions while lock files or verification metadata improve reproducibility. Avoid dynamic versions such as 1.+ in production because the same commit can resolve differently later. Use the dependency report to identify why an artifact is present before excluding it.

blocks.caption: Reports expose the resolved graph and the selection path for one dependency.

blocks.title: Offline and reproducible are different
blocks.text: A cached build may work without a network, but reproducibility also requires pinned inputs, repositories, plugins, and tool versions.

inspect.title: Read a failed task
inspect.code:
> Task :app:compileDebugKotlin FAILED
e: MainActivity.kt:18: Unresolved reference: NoteRoute
> Task :app:mergeDebugResources SKIPPED
walkthrough: The failed task names the module, variant, and compilation boundary.
The source location and unresolved symbol are the first actionable diagnostic.
A later task being skipped is a consequence, not a second root cause.
inspect.expectedOutput: Investigate NoteRoute imports, source-set inclusion, or dependencies before clearing caches.

trap_check.why: It discards valid incremental outputs and hides whether inputs are declared correctly.
trap_check.fix: Use incremental builds and clean only to test a specific stale-output hypothesis.

trap_check.why: The same commit can resolve different artifacts over time and break reproducibility.
trap_check.fix: Pin versions and update them as reviewed source changes.
